items.text: The module asked us to frame our own problem and write our own brief. That meant working through ambiguity and vagueness before there was even a problem at all.
I started wide, and probed my interest in Non-Verbal Communication, with every place communication happens without words. That eventually followed into the branch about animals and humans.

items.text: Three contexts came out of it: the street, the home and the zoo. For each, I put together a context sheet, wrote scenarios (setting, persona, trigger, action, internal state, friction) and How Might We questions, then clustered and voted on them.
Ahmedabad has about 1.5 lakh street dogs by current AMC estimates. Anti-rabies vaccinations have surged to 7,500 a month. The AMC has notified only 126 designated feeding spots for the entire city.

items.text: The urban institution and captive animals

Zoo visits are mostly about 'recognizing' and 'identifying' animals, rather than 'relating' to them. This creates a distance where visitors are disengaged, behave inappropriately in order to incite a spectacle, and animals are treated like objects of spectacle, making the visit feel shallow and disconnected.

Kankaria Zoo in Ahmedabad draws over 2 million visitors a year, up to 20,000 a day at peak, at ₹20 a ticket (₹10 for children). Ambient noise of 70–75 dB has been linked to higher cortisol and more pacing in leopards. In February 2026, the Central Zoo Authority mandated that zoos move from “display centres” to spaces for “research, learning, and inspiring empathy”.
Sources: MDPI Animals 2023; ResearchGate 2025; PIB Delhi, Feb 2026.
The HMWs clustered into animal observation and behaviour interpretation, animal welfare and autonomy, physical and spatial design, and data capture and monitoring.

items.text: Why zoo? The clearest place to design: highest density of encounters, most visible breakdown, and a live policy mandate to fix it.

Zoo visits are mostly about recognising and identifying animals, and not relating to them. This creates a distance where visitors disengage, provoke animals to trigger a reaction, and treat them as objects of spectacle.

items.text: School-aged children. 6 to 14. Organised group visits. Highest provocation rate of any visitor group. Lowest biodiversity literacy. First and often only direct encounter with these animals.
What lands here lands for life.
What the tiger is actually doing

children.text: 40–50 BPM resting heart rate. Ears rotating independently, mapping every footfall in the corridor. Vigilant acoustic mapping.
Infrasound reception: processing territorial signals below 20Hz, completely inaudible to humans. It is listening to a frequency we cannot hear.
Stereotypic pacing, zoochosis. Repetitive locomotion from spatial frustration. A coping mechanism. The zoo’s own failure, made physical.
Pinna directionality: involuntary rotation to locate and triangulate a threat source. The ear moved because a child shouted three enclosures away.
Flehmen response: drawing scent into the Jacobson’s organ to read the reproductive and social status of every animal and human in the space.

items.text: Typical visitor remarks, and the tiger’s umwelt behind them.
Leopards operate in infrasound and spatial acoustic maps imperceptible to humans. The gap is hardware.
Primary research at Indroda Nature Park and Kankaria Zoo, Ahmedabad. Tested Wizard of Oz prototypes, observational studies with field notes.

items.text: Signs, guides, and plaques address biographical illiteracy at best. Behavioural and sensorial remain mostly unattended to.
The gap is the ability to receive what the animal is already broadcasting.
How some traditions relate to animals
This knowledge existed. We designed it out. Indigenous and traditional communities did not have this gap.
Humans and animals depicted at equal scale, in shared ecological space. Cohabitation.
Western Ghats leopard and tiger deity. The animal is a presence to be respected. Territorial boundaries acknowledged before approach.
A cross-cultural practice of temporarily inhabiting an animal’s body schema to understand its state. Embodied empathy as a method.
The goal of the project then became to turn visitors from passive spectators, to actively engaged kin.

items.text: The chest contains CT afferents that route to the interoceptive cortex. The body reads the signal as coming from within. The wrist is informational touch. The chest is affective touch.

items.text: Translucent tinted polycarbonate, satin finish. Electronics visible inside.
Soft-touch silicone rubber. 5 contact points, 5 actuators.
Braided nylon. Secure handling in high-density environments.

DA7280 LRA: central pad, heartbeat + resonance.
4× ERM: toe pads, directional rhythm.
NeoPixel strip: edge, valence layer.
ESP32-C3: wireless control.
Neo6M GPS: locator.
TTP223: touch sensor for activation.
Translucent by design. The child sees it working. Transparency as consent.

Most educational media routes through the brain first; signs, screens, audio guides land in the cognitive layer, the same layer where we project narratives onto what we see. Haptics bypass that layer entirely.

Two approaches. Where a biological rhythm exists, such as a heartbeat or a breath, we mirror it directly. Where it doesn’t, we use rhythm rate and envelope shape as the emotional lever. Slow and smooth reads as calm. Fast and jagged reads as threat. The body already knows this.
Rhythm is the single parameter that independently modulates valence, arousal, and perceived roughness. Only naturalistic, biomimetic patterns reliably reach calm-pleasant states in children.
Every pattern decision was checked against research on affective haptics.

children.text: Rhythm rate shapes emotional valence far more than the carrier frequency. (Azevedo et al., 2017; Costa et al., 2016)
Calm states are reached with naturalistic rhythms like breath and heartbeat. Abstract codes fail, especially with children. (Shim & Tan, 2020)
No standard mapping between vibration patterns and emotions exists yet.

items.text: I scored candidate behaviours on Frequency (how often it happens), Gap (how invisible or misread it is to visitors) and Viability (whether it can be sensed and felt).
Pointing a phone at the animal
My first test was a phone app: point the camera at an animal, and I would Wizard-of-Oz a haptic response from a laptop. The visitors who used this seemed disconnected, the phone gets in the way.
A screen pulls the eyes away from the animal. The children need to be watching the animal in the moment, so I moved away from anything screen-based.
The first paw was cardboard: a linear actuator in the centre, coin motors for the toes and a ring of NeoPixels, driven from a Wizard of Oz panel on a laptop.

items.alt: The cardboard paw lit up in front of the Wizard of Oz panel on a laptop
The cardboard paw with its actuators taped on and wires everywhere

items.text: The cardboard paw and its Wizard of Oz panel.
I played patterns on the paw and asked people what each one made them feel.
Vibration told people how intense a state was, but not whether it was good or bad.
So I added light. Colours and light patterns are easier to understand and recognise, so the light carries what kind of state it is, and the vibration carries how strong it is.
SPANDA is also a support device for a tour guide, so nothing arrives out of context. There will be instructions as well.
Conveying an emotion through touch was more complex than I had first thought.

I needed to see a pattern to design it, so I built Haptics Studio: a timeline editor, like a music production app, for composing patterns across the five actuators and the light, and playing them on the paw as you go.

items.text: The child calibrates at entry, during a brief onboarding, to felt metaphors. Intensity set, mystery intact.
At the enclosure, GPS confirms which animal they are standing in front of. In multi-animal enclosures, one hero individual is foregrounded via signage.
The trigger is either a keeper who knows the animal’s current state, or the CV pipeline reading it live. Either way, what arrives in the child’s chest is presence.
YOLOv8 found and tracked the animal, its movement told rest apart from pacing, and a keeper could confirm or override the state from a web panel. Whatever was chosen went straight to the paw.
Next: a chain of small models
Each model has one job. Two come off the shelf; only the behaviour model is trained on SPANDA’s data.

items.alt: Camera feed, detect and track, body pose, behaviour model, state; then confident, change spotted or unsure
items.caption: How SPANDA reads the animal. Click to enlarge.

items.text: The pose model turns video into a stick figure, so the behaviour model only has to learn how that stick figure moves. That needed a few hundred labelled clips, not tens of thousands of frames.
Why not one big AI model
Sending video to a general model is slow and costly to run all day, and it only needed to stick to SPANDA’s six behaviours for the proof of concept.
Noticing that something changed is fast; naming the new state takes a few seconds. So the paw goes quiet in between, and never plays a state it is not sure of.

SPANDA is trained on individuals. Keepers log daily behavioural observations per named animal. The hero animal selected for each enclosure is the one the child will feel: ‘Prathap’, one named leopard. This is what makes attribution possible, and attribution is what makes empathy possible.

items.alt: Gather, label, train, evaluate, deploy, with the keeper in the loop
items.caption: Start from public data, then learn each named animal from the keepers who know it. Click to enlarge.

items.text: The model asks a keeper only when it is unsure, and those answers become new training examples, so it gets better at reading that one animal over time.
A trained behaviour model: coming soon.

items.text: FAQs (frequently asked to me, by me)
Highest provocation rate. Lowest literacy. Longest memory. A felt experience at 8 years old shapes how you see an animal for the rest of your life.
Sound is processed cognitively. We assign meaning, narrative, and emotion to what we hear. Haptics bypass that layer. The body receives before the brain interprets.
A screen pulls the eyes away from the animal. The point is to watch the animal in the moment.
What if the animal isn’t visible?
SPANDA defaults to resting heartbeat. Presence felt even when presence is hidden.
One hero individual foregrounded per enclosure, introduced by name via signage. SPANDA is calibrated to that individual.
CV pipeline handles it. Keeper presence enables richer contextual triggering. No keeper means the system runs autonomously. Both are valid.
How do you handle haptic subjectivity?
Metaphor-based calibration at entry sets individual intensity and sensitivity. Long term, each calibration becomes a data point for a learning model.
SPANDA supports a tour guide, so nothing arrives out of context. There will be instructions as well.
Keepers already log daily behavioural observations. SPANDA plugs into that existing workflow. Each enclosure gets a trained model per individual animal. The pipeline is repeatable.
The metaphor-based calibration exists as a concept. The kiosk interface, the child-facing flow, the sensitivity logic are all unbuilt. Designing that experience is the next design problem.

Currently a bare web panel for demo triggering. A proper keeper interface would let staff log behavioural observations in real time, flag state changes, and build the ethogram directly through daily interaction with the device. A full design project in itself.
In place of “Indian Leopard, Panthera pardus fusca”: Dharma. 7 years old. Currently resting. Signage that makes the animal a subject.
Each calibration a data point. The system gets better at knowing which patterns land for which bodies. The framework keeps getting learnt.
One that doesn’t exist yet in this project or in the literature. SPANDA is the first attempt to need one.

Directional microphones picking up vocalisation, thermal cameras reading body heat and respiration, ground vibration sensors detecting movement through substrate. More of the animal’s inner life translatable, including when it isn’t visible.
Brainstormed and ideated using the 5W + H framework. Helped in filtering what would work best for the problem at hand.

Every decision was backed by research and based on logic. 
Every intuitive call was based on my primary research.

items.text: To keep the proof of concept controlled and actionable, I narrowed it to one animal, the tiger, and studied its ethogram. From the sensory map, I shortlisted ten behaviours, then scored the candidates:

Before I settled on the zoo, I spoke to people about their relationships with animals: what they fear, why they care, and how close they like to get. Some were afraid of animals, some cared deeply, some liked to watch from a distance, and a few were activists.
Once I had picked the zoo, I spoke to zoo superintendents. They were defensive about how the zoo works.
Every sign introduced its animal the same way: a common name, a scientific name, length, weight, diet and range. At best, they present the animal as an object of scientific interest.

items.text: Conservation psychology links empathy for animals to conservation behaviour. Perspective taking, imagining the world from an animal’s point of view, is one of the ways that empathy is built.
Empathy needs an individual to care about, and a way into its point of view.

Touch can carry feeling. Rhythm shapes how a vibration feels more than its frequency does. Biological rhythms like a heartbeat or a breath read more clearly than abstract codes. And the chest is tied to affective touch in a way the wrist is not.
A rhythm felt on the chest could carry an animal’s state without words.
Seifi & MacLean, 2013; Shim & Tan, 2020; McGlone et al., 2014.
ZooWear, a head-mounted haptic interface tested in zoos, increased visitors’ sense of connection with nature. It maps food chain relationships: who is predator, and who is prey.
There was room for something that carries one animal’s inner state.
Beyond the zoo itself, I read about animal perception, empathy, affective touch and earlier zoo experiments. Each one shaped a decision.

Jakob von Uexküll called each animal’s perceptual world its umwelt: the slice of reality its senses can reach. A leopard’s includes infrasound, scent maps and an acoustic map of every footfall around it. Ours doesn’t.
I mapped what a big cat senses across nine categories, 23 traits from night vision to raised hackles, each with a way it could be simulated.
The gap between visitor and animal is biological. We aren’t equipped to perceive what they perceive.
The animal is already speaking. We just don’t have the equipment to receive it.
